The U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Justice Programs proposes creating a new Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) system of records, JUSTICE/OJP-017.  
The system would support BJS’s mission to collect, analyze, publish, and disseminate statistics on crime, victims, offenders, and criminal, civil, and administrative justice systems.  
It would contain survey responses and administrative records involving individuals such as inmates, defendants, victims, probationers, parolees, arrestees, and people involved in justice proceedings.  
Records may include identifying, criminal-history, demographic, medical, employment, financial, and contact information, but federal law limits their use to statistical and research purposes and prohibits using them for law enforcement or individual benefit determinations.  
The notice takes effect upon publication, with public comments on the system’s routine uses due by November 16, 2026.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury proposes creating a new Privacy Act system of records, “Department of the Treasury .033,” for federal student aid portfolio research, oversight, reporting, and compliance.  
Under an interagency agreement, the Department of Education will provide Treasury with personally identifiable information and other data on federal student aid recipients and borrowers from systems including NSLDS, DMCS, and EDMAPS.  
Treasury will use the information for portfolio management, research, policy development, monitoring, reporting, audits, reconciliations, compliance reviews, and coordination with oversight organizations.  
The records may include information protected under FERPA, and Treasury says it will apply access controls, auditing, training, security safeguards, and approved retention and disposal practices.  
The system becomes effective upon publication, while its routine uses take effect after 30 days, and public comments are due by November 6, 2026, through Regulations.gov or Treasury.

The Treasury Department issued a final rule amending its auction regulations for marketable book-entry Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.  
The changes update definitions and terminology, remove outdated references, and align auction rules with Treasury’s planned auction-system upgrade.  
Beginning with the upgraded system, submitters must provide each noncompetitive customer’s name and bid amount before the noncompetitive auction closes, rather than submitting only a summary amount.  
The rule also clarifies inflation-protected security calculations without changing how adjusted values, index ratios, or settlement amounts are calculated.  
Most provisions take effect October 15, 2026, while the noncompetitive-bid changes apply when the upgraded auction system begins operating.

The amendments modify requirements for submitting noncompetitive customer bids to require submitters to provide each individual customer's name and bid amount prior to the noncompetitive auction close, eliminating the ability to submit summary bid amounts.

The changes to 31 CFR 356.14 and 356.23 apply to auctions beginning with the first Treasury marketable securities auction conducted using Treasury's upgraded auction system, which will be communicated to market participants in advance.

The final rule is exempt from Administrative Procedure Act notice and comment requirements under 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(2) because the auction regulations relate to Treasury securities, which are contracts between Treasury and the security owner.

The FDA announced four Emergency Use Authorizations (EUAs) for animal products to treat or prevent infestations by New World screwworm larvae.  
Elanco’s CLiK Extra was authorized for wound application in livestock and certain wildlife, while Zoetis’s Simparica TRIO was authorized to treat infestations in dogs and puppies.  
Bimeda’s Bimectin was authorized to prevent infestations in cattle, and Sergeant’s CAPSTAR was authorized to treat and prevent infestations in dogs, puppies, cats, and kittens meeting specified age and weight requirements.  
The EUAs were issued between August 7 and September 3, 2026, and include conditions governing emergency use.  
They followed an August 18, 2025, HHS determination and declaration that New World screwworm posed a significant potential public health and national-security threat, with FDA concluding that the products’ potential benefits outweighed their risks and that no adequate approved alternatives were available.

The article introduces DiffTry, a stateless retry mechanism that gives high-priority microservice requests more retry attempts than low-priority requests.  
By applying priority at the rejection point, DiffTry protects valuable transactions during overload while limiting retry storms, unnecessary scaling, and resource waste.  
The authors develop analytical models for single services and general service networks to estimate throughput, rejection rates, completion probabilities, and the effects of different retry limits.  
Their analysis shows that increasing retry limits for important request classes improves their success rates monotonically, with especially strong guarantees for networks whose service-flow graphs are acyclic.  
Simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment confirm the model’s predictions and demonstrate that DiffTry can be deployed as a service-mesh plugin without application changes or centralized coordination.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.

The FAA issued a final airworthiness directive for certain Bombardier BD-700-2A12 airplanes after reports of insufficient clearance among right-wing fuel, hydraulic, vent, and harness components.  
If unaddressed, the conditions could create an ignition source in a fuel tank during a lightning strike.  
Effective November 18, 2026, the directive requires replacing a harness-support clip-nut and fuel-tube assemblies, inspecting clearances, and replacing hydraulic-system support brackets if needed.  
The FAA rejected requests for an emergency directive, shorter compliance times, or additional technical analyses, stating the risk does not involve fuel starvation or a system failure.  
The rule affects an estimated 60 U.S.-registered airplanes, with required actions costing about $2,693 per aircraft, or $161,580 total, though warranties may reduce operators’ expenses.

summary_responses.subtopic: Public Administration, Labor Policy & Family Leave
summary_responses.response: The Office of Personnel Management is issuing a direct final rule updating its Family and Medical Leave Act regulations to reflect statutory amendments enacted in 2021 and 2023. The changes make virtually all civilian federal service—including temporary and intermittent service—count toward the 12-month FMLA eligibility requirement, while still requiring employees to meet other coverage criteria. They also allow qualifying honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward eligibility, but exclude Coast Guard and Public Health Service commissioned corps service. The rule clarifies that annual and sick leave provided under non-title 5 authorities may replace unpaid FMLA leave and removes Veterans Health Administration employees covered under a separate leave system from title 5 FMLA coverage. It is scheduled to take effect December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are submitted by November 16, 2026, and the changes also affect eligibility for federal paid parental leave.
